1.text: The religious ideas of both branches of the Chukchee are so much alike,

2.text: that they can be described together.¹ Minor differences will be pointed out

4.text: In studying the religious ideas of the Chukchee I gradually formed a

5.text: simple theory about the first development of the religious concepts of primitive

6.text: man in general. I give it here, in the beginning of this chapter, in order to

7.text: make what follows easier to understand. Its value for me is the help it was

8.text: to me in arranging the material in a systematic way.

9.text: Primitive man, conscious of life, which is the source of his actions, attrib-

10.text: utes similar life and inherent virtue to all surrounding objects of nature that

11.text: have attracted his attention by their activity, by some striking feature of their

12.text: outward appearance, or, indeed, by any other circumstance. This attribution

13.text: of life similar to his own² forms the basis of his religious concepts; and

14.text: primitive mythology develops from it by gradual ramification and working-up

16.text: STAGES OF DEVELOPMENT OF PRIMITIVE RELIGIOUS CONCEPTS. — The primary

17.text: development of the attribution of life here described presents five stages, more

18.text: or less distinct, which are as follows: —

19.text: The first stage relates only to that qualitative similarity of man and objects

20.text: which consists in the belief that life is their common property. The form of the

22.text: ¹ The material presented in this chapter was collected principally from shamans, and aged people versed

23.text: in “old tidings” (teleˊnkin pɪˊñɪltê), as the Chukchee call everything relating to their mythology or history.

24.text: These data were supplemented from their folk-tales, to which, in many cases, no specific references can be given,

25.text: since the larger part of them are not yet published. The tales, however, were used only so far as they yielded

26.text: new details regarding the characters and mythical beings known to the Chukchee. Stories like those about the

27.text: creation of the world and the part that the raven and other birds and animals played in it will be treated

29.text: The Chukchee conception of various supernatural beings treated of in this chapter is illustrated by a

30.text: number of pencil-sketches which I requested several natives in various parts of the country to make for me.

31.text: It seemed to me that graphic representation of things previously described merely in words would add new

32.text: details which otherwise would be out of the reach of the investigator. Care was taken, in comparing details

33.text: given by different men, to eliminate those differing from the general character of the description. Nevertheless,

34.text: the sketches remain individual, and they are of scientific value only so far as they help to an understanding of

35.text: the forms which present themselves to the mind of the Chukchee. I shall speak of them again when referring

36.text: to Chukchee art; but I take up a few of them here to illustrate the religious ideas of the people.

37.text: ² I avoid using the term “animism,” because it presupposes the conception of the human soul, which,

38.text: in my opinion, belongs to a later stage. E. B. Tylor says that animism includes two great dogmas, forming

39.text: parts of one consistent doctrine; first, concerning souls of individual creatures capable of continued existence

40.text: after the death or destruction of the body; second, concerning other spirits, upward to the rank of powerful

41.text: deities (Primitive Culture, p. 426). According to my theory, these two dogmas belong to the last stage of

42.text: development. On the whole, my plan must be considered as an attempt to outline the way in which primitive

43.text: man (Chukchee) reached the stage of animism.
